findings.suggestion: On a scratch worktree, revert only implement's three normalisation hunks - HostNormalizer's body, UrlValidator.requireShortenable (129-131), DenylistThreatCheck.evaluate (55-64) - and run HostEvasionRefusalTest and HostCanonicalisationTest against the current test tree. Attach the failing output (expect aDenylistedHostWithATrailingDotIsRefusedIdenticallyToTheHostItself and anInternalAddressWrittenAsOneDecimalNumberIsRefusedIdenticallyToTheDottedForm red) to the run record as AC3's evidence, or have a human waive the ordering constraint explicitly. Listed first among the blockers because the remedy is purely mechanical and can be completed in one sitting, unlike SEC-1. Note this is an evidence gap, not a defect in the change: the code under test is, by every other lens's reading, correct. Do not close it by relaxing AC3 or by citing the green post-fix suite - a green suite is precisely the artefact AC3 says is insufficient. Related: TEST-3 and TEST-6 record two further pieces of new behaviour that no test can currently see, so the suite's discriminating power is weaker in this area than the 110 new methods suggest.
findings.summary: PROMOTED by synthesis from major to blocker: the test lens filed this as major, but it is an unmet AC deliverable that a downstream node will otherwise assert as met, and the promotion exists so a human adjudicates rather than inherits it. AC3 has two halves and only one is evidenced. The tests exist and are retained, but 'fail against the pre-change code' was never observed: the run journal shows author-tests and implement started in parallel (seq 71-72), author-tests' exit gates were tests_compile / tests_not_weakened / paths_confined with no execution, and the first suite run was maven_verify at the verify node, after the join - i.e. only ever against the fixed code. plan.json's T1 names 'run log entry recording the failing run against pre-change code' as a deliverable and there is no such entry; test-contract.json's own rationale flagged this as 'a pipeline obligation... the single easiest thing here to lose'. By inspection the test does discriminate (pre-change, requireShortenable lower-cased the raw host and DenylistThreatCheck matched the raw host, so https://malware.example.com./x returned 201), but 'by inspection' is exactly what AC3 refuses.

findings.suggestion: Decide explicitly whether an account of age zero may take a link down. Cheapest closures that need no new subsystem: (a) require the reporter's account to pre-date the reported link, or to be older than some app.abuse.min-reporter-age; (b) queue rather than block when the reporter has no links of their own, so the immediate-takedown power stays with established accounts; or (c) add a second bucket keyed by client address alongside the customer-id bucket, so minting accounts does not multiply takedown capacity. Whichever is chosen, add a test to SignUpIsolationTest asserting the outcome of a fresh account reporting another customer's code - that assertion is currently absent and is the security control this finding is about. Read this together with SEC-2 (the sign-up bucket, the only bound on account minting, evaporates entirely when Redis is unreachable) and SEC-5 (if the edge proxy does not preserve the source address, the per-IP bound is a single global bucket and option (c) buys nothing). Option (c) is therefore the weakest of the three unless SEC-5 is resolved first. Separately, impact.json's 'low' rating for this data flow should be re-rated as part of adjudicating this finding; no lens filed that as a finding because it is a pipeline artefact rather than code.
findings.summary: PROMOTED by synthesis from major to blocker: the security lens filed major, but the capability is cross-tenant, immediate, unmoderated and irreversible by design (no unblock path, explicitly out of scope), it becomes reachable by anyone only because of this change, and the recorded risk assessment for it is now demonstrably wrong - that combination needs a person, not a reviewer's judgement call. Self-service sign-up silently re-scopes every authenticated endpoint from 'two hand-provisioned accounts' to 'anyone on the internet', and the one authenticated capability that deliberately crosses tenant boundaries is the abuse-report takedown. I confirmed by reading report(): it resolves by (domain, code) with no owner scoping and immediately markBlocked()s the link, with no moderation queue. The only defence is ABUSE_REPORT keyed by customer id at 60/min - and after this change an attacker mints customer ids at 60/min per IP through POST /api/v1/customers, so the per-reporter bucket bounds nothing. Any published short link (and short links are published by definition) can now be permanently killed by an unauthenticated stranger who spends one sign-up. impact.json recorded this data flow as risk 'low' on the stated basis that 'only signed-in callers can report', which AC4 makes vacuous; SignUpIsolationTest pins that a new account cannot read/modify/delete/list another customer's link but does not pin what it can do to one via abuse-reports.

findings.suggestion: Make the fail-open decision per bucket rather than global: keep ALLOWED-on-error for CLICK and NOT_FOUND (a 429'd redirect is a self-inflicted outage), and fail closed with 503 service_unavailable for SIGN_UP. That is the same shape AC15 already asks for - degradation spent on refusing new writes, never on serving clicks - and it makes the sign-up path behave under a Redis outage the way the anonymous-create path already does. A boolean on RateLimitBucket, or a set of buckets consulted in the catch at line 67, is enough. Placed first among the majors despite medium confidence because it is load-bearing for the SEC-1 blocker and for the quantitative bounds cited in SEC-7 and PERF-2: every 'bounded at N/min' claim in this review is conditional on Redis being up, and this is the one change that makes that conditional false only for the paths where being throttled is safe. Note that no lens read redis/token_bucket.lua, so the limiter's behaviour under partial failure (as distinct from unreachable) is asserted from the Java call site only.
findings.summary: The limiter fails open on an unreachable Redis (deliberate, pre-existing, and correct for the click path). Anonymous link creation is incidentally protected from that during a Redis outage because ResolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing throws 503 before a row is written. POST /api/v1/customers has no such gate: it touches only PostgreSQL, so with Redis down it is completely unmetered - unbounded 16 MiB/~25 ms Argon2id hashes (Tomcat's 200 default threads x 16 MiB is ~3.2 GiB), unbounded customer rows, and unbounded account minting, which compounds SEC-1 exactly when the operator is already busy. The requirement's non-functional list says an unauthenticated endpoint that writes to the database must not become an unmetered storage-burn vector; today the only thing enforcing that on sign-up is a dependency the design documents as fail-open. Two lenses converged on this fail-open behaviour from different directions - security as the loss of the only bound on account minting, performance (PERF-2) as the loss of the only bound on concurrent memory-hard hashing - which is why it is listed ahead of the findings it undermines.

findings.suggestion: Make the constraint and the query agree: either add `CREATE INDEX ix_customers_upper_email ON customers (upper(email))`, or change the finder to an explicit JPQL `where lower(c.email) = lower(:email)` so the lower(email) index serves both roles. The JPQL option is preferable - it removes an index rather than adding one, and it makes the read path and the uniqueness constraint agree on a single canonical form, which is the same equivalent-form discipline HostNormalizer applies to hosts. Confirm before shipping by turning on spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.show_sql in a test run to capture the generated predicate, then EXPLAIN it against a customers table seeded with ~100k rows and check for Index Scan rather than Seq Scan. Listed first among the performance majors because the fix is small, mechanical and verifiable in one sitting, and because it is the only finding here whose cost lands on an existing endpoint (sign-in) rather than on the new ones.
findings.summary: The new unique index is on lower(email), but the only query that reads by email is CustomerRepository.findByEmailIgnoreCase, which Spring Data renders as `where upper(c.email) = upper(?)`. A functional index on lower(email) cannot serve an upper() predicate, and ux_customers_email (plain email) cannot serve it either, so sign-in seq-scans customers on every attempt. That was cheap while customers held two seeded rows; this change makes the table grow without bound from an unauthenticated endpoint, so sign-in latency now grows linearly with sign-up volume, and sign-in is already the slowest endpoint in the service (an Argon2 verify runs on every attempt, including unknown accounts). The index is correct as a constraint; it is just not the index the read path needs. I confirmed both halves independently of the lens: V3 line 27 is `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX ux_customers_lower_email ON customers (lower(email))`, and CustomerRepository.java:26 is the derived finder `Optional<CustomerEntity> findByEmailIgnoreCase(String email)` with no @Query override.

findings.suggestion: Take the cache invalidation off the open transaction - commit the insert, then invalidate before returning (the pre-issue ordering still holds relative to the response) - or at minimum set spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size explicitly against expected concurrency and document the interaction. Confirm by running the existing AnonymousCreateDegradationTest variant with Redis latency injected (e.g. a proxy adding 800 ms) while watching hikaricp_connections_pending and redirect p99 on /actuator/prometheus. Unlike SEC-3, this finding does not depend on Hibernate's connection-acquisition mode: saveAndFlush has already issued SQL by the time the Redis call is made, so a physical connection is definitely held under either mode. Note the coupling to TEST-2: the invalidateBeforeIssuing call is exactly the one whose removal TEST-2 shows the suite would not notice, so whoever restructures this ordering should fix TEST-2 first, or the restructure ships with no test that can see it went wrong.
findings.summary: createAnonymous holds an open database transaction across a Redis round trip: saveAndFlush inserts the row, then resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing does a network call to Redis with a 1s timeout, all inside @Transactional. The connection pool is Hikari at its default maximum of 10 (I confirmed nothing in application.yml sizes it). When Redis is slow rather than down - the common failure - each create pins a pooled connection for up to ~1s in the evict alone, plus up to ~1s more in the rate-limit call before the handler is entered; ten concurrent creates exhaust the pool and the redirect path's cache-miss fallback to PostgreSQL then queues behind them. The failure is self-amplifying: a degraded Redis makes the limiter fail open, so the anonymous endpoint becomes unmetered at precisely the moment each request is holding a connection for a second. The shape is pre-existing in create(), but create() is authenticated and customer-bucketed; this replicates it on an unauthenticated, IP-bucketed path.

findings.suggestion: Bound the hashing work rather than only metering the callers: put sign-up (and ideally sign-in) hashing behind a Semaphore or a fixed executor sized to the available cores, refusing with 429/503 past the queue rather than accumulating threads. Measure by running N concurrent sign-ups (N = 2x cores and 10x cores) while sampling redirect p99 in the same process; the number that matters is redirect latency under sign-up load, not sign-up throughput. Also record the JVM heap/container memory headroom against 200 x 16 MiB in the runbook. Placed last among the majors because it is the only one with no small mechanical fix - it needs a capacity decision and a measurement, and no lens had any traffic figures to size it with. If only one of PERF-2 and SEC-2 is done, SEC-2 is the better buy: it restores the bound in the state where it matters most, whereas a semaphore alone still lets an unmetered flood queue.
findings.summary: POST /api/v1/customers puts an Argon2id hash (m=16384 KiB, t=2, ~25 ms, 16 MiB transient per call) on an unauthenticated path with no global concurrency bound. Tomcat's default 200 request threads means a worst case of ~200 concurrent hashes, i.e. ~3.2 GiB of transient allocation and full CPU saturation in the same JVM that serves the redirect path, which has no CPU isolation from it. The only defence is the per-IP SIGN_UP bucket at 60/min, which (a) does not bound aggregate concurrency across many source addresses and (b) fails open by design when Redis is unreachable, so the vector is fully open in exactly the degraded state where the service is least able to absorb it. The duplicate-sign-up path pays the full hash before the constraint refuses it, so a repeat flood against one known address costs the same as real sign-ups. Sign-in already has this shape, so this is a second equal entry point rather than a new class of problem - but it doubles it, and it is the one being added. The security lens reached the same exposure via SEC-2 (unmetered under Redis outage) and SEC-3 (cost paid inside a transaction); those are kept separate because each has a different fix, but all three describe one CPU/memory budget with no ceiling on it.

findings.suggestion: Extract `private URI acceptableTarget(String longUrl)` containing the three calls and have both create and createAnonymous call it. The design's reason for two public methods (different request/response types, different expiry) is unaffected - only the shared acceptance rule moves. Worth noting that this is the same class of hazard TEST-6 records from the other side: there, a security property holds only because two components run in a particular order; here, a security property holds only because two methods happen to spell the same sequence. Neither is currently wrong; both are one edit away from being wrong, and in both cases no test would notice.
findings.summary: The three-call target-acceptance sequence (parseOrThrow / requireShortenable / requirePermittedTarget) is now written twice, in create and createAnonymous. AC12 requires the two paths to accept exactly the same targets, and the javadoc on createAnonymous asserts that in prose, but nothing in the code enforces it: a fourth check added to create in six months is silently absent from the anonymous path. This is duplication of the kind that drifts, and it is the security-relevant kind. Listed first among the minors because it is the cheapest structural change in the review and because it is the only one that protects an acceptance criterion from future edits rather than fixing a present defect - the two paths do agree today.

findings.suggestion: Fail fast at bean construction: if ownHost is non-null and does not normalise, throw IllegalStateException from the UrlValidator constructor so a misconfigured base-url stops the context at startup rather than quietly turning off a check nobody will notice is off. If failing startup is judged too aggressive, the minimum both lenses would accept is a single log.warn naming the host and stating that the self-referential check is inactive. Both lenses proposed constructor-time failure independently. Note the interaction with TEST-3: no test can currently see the own-host check at all, because every context boots with app.base-url=http://localhost:8080 and localhost is refused by the internal-address rule regardless - so whichever behaviour is chosen here, the unit test TEST-3 asks for (`new UrlValidator("short.example")`) is the same test that would pin it, and the two should be fixed together.
findings.summary: MERGED: the security and cleanliness lenses independently found the same defect at the same line, which is itself evidence - two reviewers with different briefs both stopped at it. `canonicalOwnHost = HostNormalizer.normalize(ownHost).orElse(null)` silently disables the self-referential-target check when the configured own host cannot be canonicalised, and line 130 then skips the check because canonicalOwnHost is null. Security's framing: that is a fail-open inside a class whose documented contract two lines earlier is that an un-canonicalisable host fails closed; reachable only through a misconfigured app.base-url, and the loopback rules would still catch the default localhost, so the practical exposure is small - a short link pointing at our own origin, i.e. a redirect loop through us (severity nit as filed). Cleanliness's framing: the degradation is silent - no log line, no failure - so the only symptom is short links pointing at short links, and elsewhere this codebase is careful to log the moment a protection stops applying (the fail-open warn in LinkService.requirePermittedTarget, JwtSessionService's ephemeral-key warning), which made it minor as filed. Merged severity is the higher of the two, minor.

findings.suggestion: Hash before the transaction opens: compute the encoded hash in the controller or in a non-transactional method and pass it into a small @Transactional insert, so the connection is held only for the saveAndFlush. Behaviour, including the 409-from-constraint semantics, is unchanged. This is worth doing regardless of how the acquisition-mode question resolves - it is a few lines, it makes the code correct under either mode, and it removes the need to reason about the default at all. If instead someone wants to close this by argument, the thing to verify is one line of evidence: log or assert the acquisition mode (or watch hikaricp_connections_active during a sign-up burst). That same evidence decides whether PERF-2 is worse than filed, so it is worth capturing once.
findings.summary: passwordHasher.hash() runs inside the @Transactional signUp method, so - on the security lens's reading - each unauthenticated sign-up holds a pooled JDBC connection for the ~25 ms of memory-hard Argon2id work before it does any SQL. At the configured 60/min per IP (and unbounded per SEC-2) this starves the HikariCP pool, and the pool is shared with the click path's PostgreSQL fallback on a resolution-cache miss - the one path the requirement says degradation must never be spent on. SignInService has the same shape, so this is a pattern rather than a novelty, but sign-up doubles the exposed surface and adds a write. SYNTHESIS NOTE - two lenses disagree here and a human should settle it: the performance lens explicitly listed Hibernate's physical connection handling mode as assumed-not-verified, saying that if acquisition is eager the hash runs while holding a connection and PERF-2/PERF-3 would upgrade. I read the code and the config: the hash is genuinely inside the transaction and precedes all SQL (saveAndFlush is the first statement), and application.yml sets no hibernate connection-handling key, so Spring Boot's default DELAYED_ACQUISITION_AND_RELEASE_AFTER_TRANSACTION applies - under which no physical connection is held during the hash and the pool-starvation mechanism described here does not fire. I am keeping the finding at its filed severity rather than downgrading on my own reading, because the whole argument turns on one framework default that nobody has observed.

findings.suggestion: Prepend `SET lock_timeout = '3s';` to V4 (and to V3) so the migration fails fast and retryably rather than queueing readers behind it, and note in the deploy runbook that the retry is expected behaviour. Confirm the lock class with `SELECT mode FROM pg_locks` during a rehearsal on a copy carrying production-sized links. Placed high among the minors because it is two lines in files that are already being changed, and because it is the only deploy-time finding whose failure mode lands on the redirect path. Note it wants deciding alongside API-4, which argues the two migrations should be renumbered into the order the contract pins - both are edits to the same two files and should be made in one pass, not two.
findings.summary: ALTER TABLE links ALTER COLUMN customer_id DROP NOT NULL is a catalogue-only change and rewrites nothing, but it still needs an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on links. Flyway runs it at application startup with no lock_timeout, so if any in-flight statement holds even a weak lock on links, the ALTER waits - and while it waits, every subsequent query on links queues behind it, including the redirect path's cache-miss fallback. The blast is bounded by the cache absorbing most reads for 60 seconds, but the mechanism turns a fast DDL into a stall on the hot table with no ceiling. V3's CREATE UNIQUE INDEX (not CONCURRENTLY) has the same shape against customers: it blocks writes on customers for the duration of the build, which is trivial today at two rows and stops being trivial once sign-up has been live a while.

findings.suggestion: Replace the loop with a single `boolean existsByHostIn(Collection<String> candidates)` over the pre-computed parent chain (at most ~6 entries, bounded by label count), turning N round trips into one. Nothing about the label-based matching semantics changes - and the security lens separately confirmed that the label walk cannot collapse a public host onto a denylisted parent, so the semantics being preserved are the right ones. If this is changed, TEST-6's suggested direct unit test on DenylistThreatCheck.evaluate becomes more valuable, since the rewrite touches the method whose fail-closed branch is currently unreachable from any endpoint.
findings.summary: isListed issues one existsByHost query per label of the host: a.b.c.example.com costs five sequential database round trips, and each create pays this before it inserts. The rows are index-hits so each is cheap, but the round trips are serialised inside the create transaction and this change puts the same loop on an unauthenticated endpoint at 30/min/IP. Creates are not the hot path, so this is latency on a low-volume route rather than a capacity problem - filed because the fix is one line and the loop is now reachable without a credential. It also lengthens the window that PERF-3 is about, since these round trips happen inside the same transaction that later waits on Redis.

findings.suggestion: Reject or strip control characters from {code} before it is logged or stored - the alias/code alphabet is base62, so a single guard in the controller (or an AliasPolicy-style character check) both closes this and costs nothing. Alternatively configure a log encoder that escapes newlines, which closes the RedirectController instance at the same time and is the better buy if there are other interpolated user values elsewhere. Worth noting that the log line is also the only forensic record the abuse path produces, which is the same observability surface SEC-6 finds missing on anonymous creates - a reviewer looking at incident-response quality should read the two together.
findings.summary: The {code} path variable is percent-decoded by Spring before it reaches this log line, so POST /api/v1/links/%0aWHATEVER/abuse-reports forges an arbitrary extra line into the application log and still answers 202 (the endpoint accepts any well-formed code by design, so nothing rejects it first). RedirectController line 88 has the same shape in its catch block. This is pre-existing code that this change did not touch - it is reported because open sign-up moves it from 'reachable by two provisioned accounts' to 'reachable by anyone', which is the trust-boundary shift SEC-1 is about. I confirmed the log statement is the last line of report() and interpolates the raw code.

findings.suggestion: Log the client address on the anonymous create path (it is already in hand at PublicLinkController line 54 and is the key the bucket is charged against), or pass it into createAnonymous for the log line only. This is deliberately not a proposal to store it on the row - a log line gives incident response a handle without adding a personal-data column to links. Caveat from SEC-5: if the edge proxy does not preserve the source address, the logged value is the proxy for every request and this buys nothing, so SEC-5 should be resolved first or this fix should be sequenced behind it.
findings.summary: An anonymously created link records no attribution at all: customer_id is NULL by design, and the log line is 'Created anonymous link {code}' with no client address. When one of these links turns out to be a phishing redirect there is nothing to trace it to and no way to find the creator's other links, so the only response available is per-code abuse reports - which is the one takedown route that requires an account (SEC-1) and which nobody can use without already holding the code. The requirement asks that new behaviour be observable through the existing logging surface. This is the operational counterpart of SEC-1: that finding is about a takedown power that is too easy to obtain, this one is about the only takedown route for anonymous links being unusable at scale.

findings.suggestion: Add a behaviour whose only outcome is the refusal - e.g. anonymousCreateIsRefusedWith503WhenTheCacheCannotBeInvalidated - asserting exactly 503, error=service_unavailable and message 'Temporarily unable to accept new links.' with the counter tier paused, rather than tolerating the success. If a 201 genuinely remains permissible for the shared tier, drive the outage at the dependency the pre-issue invalidation actually needs so one answer is determined. This is more urgent than its severity suggests once PERF-3 is read alongside it: PERF-3's recommended fix is to move that same invalidateBeforeIssuing call out of the transaction, and SEC-2 observes that this 503 is the only thing that keeps anonymous create metered during a Redis outage. So the call this test cannot see is both about to be moved and load-bearing for a security property - fix the test before the restructure, not after.
findings.summary: The behaviour named for AC15 cannot fail on the thing AC15 asks for. anonymousCreationIsRefusedWithTheExistingErrorWhileADependencyIsUnavailable accepts `201 || 503`, and its three following assertions on the service_unavailable envelope are filtered on `statusCode() != 201` / `== 503`, so they are all vacuous when the answer is 201. Delete `resolutionCache.invalidateBeforeIssuing(...)` from LinkService.createAnonymous - the one call that produces the 503 there - and this test still passes. The guarantee survives only through bothCreatePathsDegradeTheSameWay, which compares the two paths' statuses; that single equality is the whole pin, and the same disjunctive tolerance on the authenticated path was already recorded as a finding in the previous run's review-test-adequacy.json.

findings.suggestion: A unit test in com.example.urlshortener.unit - UrlValidator is deliberately constructible without Spring (LinkPolicyConfig's javadoc says so) - e.g. ownHostIsRefusedInEverySpelling: `new UrlValidator("short.example")` and assert url_rejected for https://short.example./x and https://SHORT.Example/x, and no exception for https://notshort.example/x. Optionally the HTTP counterpart with app.base-url=https://short.example overridden on its own context. Write this together with the merged SEC-10/CLEAN-3 fix: the same non-localhost constructor argument that makes this behaviour visible is what makes the silent-null fail-open visible, so one new test class covers both, and after SEC-10 is fixed a third case (a base-url host that does not canonicalise) becomes assertable too.
findings.summary: New behaviour with no test that can see it: the self-referential check now compares canonical hosts (canonicalOwnHost, computed once in the constructor) so that a trailing-dot or numeric spelling of the shortener's own host is refused. No test distinguishes it. app.base-url is http://localhost:8080 in every context the suite boots, so ownHost is 'localhost', and isInternal('localhost') returns true regardless - every spelling of the own host is refused by the internal-address rule whether or not canonicalisation happens. Revert line 130 to the previous `host.equals(ownHost.toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT))` and the suite stays green; Fixtures.SELF_REFERENTIAL_URL (http://localhost:8080/somewhere) does not separate the two rules either.

findings.suggestion: Give this class a longer override (e.g. app.links.anonymous-ttl=PT10S) so the mid-life click has seconds of margin rather than a fraction of one, or assert the 302 only after re-reading the clock on the response and failing with a message that names the elapsed time. Do not relax the 302 expectation itself. Note that the margin analysis assumes a healthy Redis; the same 1s command timeout is what PERF-3 says can be consumed entirely by a slow dependency, so on a loaded CI box the true margin is smaller than the arithmetic above suggests. This is the finding in the review most likely to turn into a muted test six months from now, which is why it is filed above the documentation minors despite being a test-only concern.
findings.summary: Timing slack too thin for the click path this suite runs. The class configures a 3-second anonymous TTL and anAnonymousLinkRedirectsUntilItsExpiryPasses sleeps half of it, then requires a click to return 302. The guard `halfWay.isBefore(link.expiresAt())` is read before the request is sent, so a click that straddles the expiry passes the guard and fails on the 302 - and a served redirect makes up to three sequential Redis round trips each carrying the configured 1s command timeout, against ~1.4s of remaining margin. This is the one behaviour pinning 'live for the whole period it was promised' (AC10); if it flakes it gets muted and takes that claim with it.

findings.suggestion: Either renumber so the nullable relaxation runs first, as the contract states, or amend note 7 to record the order actually shipped and why. The human on the migration diff needs the two to agree. Synthesis view: renumbering is the better option, because the shipped order makes the failure mode strictly worse - the migration most likely to fail (the one that aborts on pre-existing duplicate addresses, a precondition the test lens notes is unfalsifiable from this repository and already recorded in docs/TODO.md) runs first, and its failure leaves the new anonymous path broken in a database that has otherwise started. Reversing the order means a V3 failure leaves a database where only the new sign-up path is unavailable. If the files are being renumbered anyway, apply PERF-6's lock_timeout in the same edit.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml note 7 (lines 249-252) pins the order of the two schema changes: 'relax links.customer_id to nullable, and add a unique index over lower(email)', in that order. The implementation ships them the other way round - I confirmed V3 is the unique index and V4 the nullable relaxation. Note 7 also warns that the lower(email) index fails to apply where duplicates exist; on the shipped order that failure aborts Flyway before customer_id is relaxed, so a partially-migrated database is one where the anonymous-create path's column constraint is still NOT NULL. The 409 account_unavailable contract depends on the V3 index existing, so the dependency itself is satisfied.

findings.suggestion: Fix the document, not the code: the 400-vs-422 split is pinned elsewhere in the contract and the blind test branch reached the same reading (Fixtures.UNPARSEABLE_OUT_OF_RANGE_NUMERIC_URL, 'No host from URI: 400'). Replace the `999.999.999.999` / empty-label examples in the 422 paragraph with `4294967296`, and say explicitly that out-of-range forms URI cannot parse remain 400. Two independent lenses converged on the code's reading here - the contract lens by compiling HostNormalizer and checking URI.getHost(), the test lens by finding the same 400 expectation already frozen in the test fixtures - which is unusually strong evidence that the document is the thing that is wrong. Note the contract file is a frozen artefact, so changing it is a contract amendment and needs whoever ratifies openapi.yaml, not the implement node.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml lines 79-82 ('Host policy and equivalent forms') and the 422 description at line 704 name `999.999.999.999` and 'an empty label' as hosts that 'cannot be canonicalised unambiguously' and are 'refused with 422 url_rejected, never accepted and never downgraded to 400'. They are in fact 400 invalid_request: java.net.URI.getHost() returns null for `http://999.999.999.999/`, `http://a..b/` and `http://1.2.3.4.5/` (verified on the same JDK 21.0.12 the pom targets), so parseOrThrow refuses them before requireShortenable/HostNormalizer ever runs. The spec contradicts itself - lines 98-101 say forms URI cannot parse a host from stay 400 - and the code follows the second sentence. Only hosts URI does parse and the normaliser then rejects (e.g. `http://4294967296/`) actually reach 422; that path works. This is the most consequential divergence found by the contract lens, and it is documentary rather than behavioural.

findings.suggestion: Either document the exception - '405 and 415 carry the framework's default body and are not part of the ApiError catalogue' - or add handlers mapping them onto ApiError (which needs a new catalogue entry, so it is a contract change). The contract lens recommends documenting, since the closed catalogue has no code that means 'method not allowed'; I would add that the 500 case deserves separate thought from the 405/415 case, because an unhandled exception reaching BasicErrorController is the one of the three where the default body's contents are not fully predictable. Note this finding and API-3 are the same decision viewed twice - both are about what the framework does on verbs the contract deliberately left undeclared on newly unauthenticated paths - and should be settled together in one amendment to the 'Three surfaces' section.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml line 121 states 'Every non-2xx response has the ApiError shape' and the catalogue is closed, but there is no handler for HttpRequestMethodNotSupportedException, HttpMediaTypeNotSupportedException or a generic Exception. The 405 the spec explicitly requires on the two new exempt paths (lines 58-61) therefore carries Spring's BasicErrorController body - {"timestamp":...,"status":405,"error":"Method Not Allowed","path":"/api/v1/customers"} - not ApiError. Same for 415 on a wrong Content-Type and 500 on anything unhandled. Newly consequential because 405 on /api/v1/customers and /api/v1/public/links is now reachable with no credentials at all, and the default body echoes the request path.

findings.suggestion: Add one sentence to the 'Three surfaces' section recording that OPTIONS on the exempt paths answers 200 with an Allow header, or set spring.mvc.dispatch-options-request=false if the intent was 405 for every non-POST verb. Decide it rather than leave it to the default. Settle alongside API-2. The security lens's not_examined records that CORS was outside its reach entirely, so if any CORS policy is ever added at the edge, this OPTIONS behaviour is the surface it will interact with - worth one sentence now rather than a surprise later. Note also the contract lens left one adjacent question unowned: whether an exempt path with odd encoding (trailing slash, %2e, matrix parameters) still matches the exact-equality exemption. Nobody examined that.
findings.summary: openapi.yaml lines 57-61 say the exemption is not method-aware and that non-POST verbs on /api/v1/customers and /api/v1/public/links 'must reach Spring's dispatcher and answer 405'. OPTIONS is not one of the four verbs listed and, with Spring MVC's default dispatchOptionsRequest=true, an unauthenticated `OPTIONS /api/v1/customers` answers 200 with `Allow: POST,OPTIONS` rather than 405 - undocumented behaviour on a path that is outside the session filter (the same request against /api/v1/links is 401, so the two new paths behave differently). Confidence is medium because this rests on a framework default rather than on code in this diff - and I confirmed application.yml sets no spring.mvc.dispatch-options-request key, so the default does apply.

findings.suggestion: Either write the deployment precondition into docs/OPERATIONS.md (the proxy must preserve the source address, e.g. PROXY protocol, or these limits are global ceilings and 30/min will be hit by ordinary traffic), or add a configurable trusted-proxy list so X-Forwarded-For can be honoured only from known hops. Note application.yml is a protected path, so a config-side fix needs a human either way. Read this before the two rate-limit majors: if the proxy does not preserve the address, then SEC-2 and PERF-2 are worse than filed (a single bucket for the whole internet, not one per attacker) and AC14 is not met at all. The test lens independently reports it cannot verify the per-caller property either, since every test in the suite originates from loopback - so the keying is unverified from both the deployment side and the test side.
findings.summary: Both new unauthenticated buckets key on httpRequest.getRemoteAddr() and deliberately do not trust X-Forwarded-For (a sound default with no trusted-proxy list). The requirement states the service sits behind an edge proxy. If that proxy terminates the connection without a PROXY-protocol or trusted-header path, getRemoteAddr() is the proxy for every request, so ANONYMOUS_CREATE (30/min) and SIGN_UP (60/min) become service-wide ceilings: one caller can consume the entire anonymous-create budget and deny the new feature to everybody, and neither bucket provides any per-attacker protection - which is the whole of what AC14 asks it for. The design explicitly deferred this to the runbook; docs/OPERATIONS.md was edited in this change and does not mention it, so the stated mitigation does not exist. This finding is a precondition for several others: SEC-1's option (c), SEC-2's and PERF-2's per-IP bounds, and SEC-6's attribution log all assume getRemoteAddr() identifies a caller.

findings.suggestion: If the oracle is accepted, tighten signUpPerMinute well below the sign-in bucket (they defend different things: sign-in throttles guesses at one known account, sign-up throttles enumeration of all of them) and close SEC-2 so the bound cannot evaporate. If it is not accepted, that is a contract change and belongs with whoever ratifies artifacts/openapi.yaml, not with implement. Synthesis view: this is an explicit open question the design node routed to review, so it needs a named decision rather than a fix, and it should be adjudicated in the same sitting as SEC-1 - both are consequences of AC4 opening the account boundary, and both were assessed on premises about rate limiting that SEC-2 and SEC-5 undermine. Note the security lens also flagged that it did not measure whether sign-up leaks existence by timing as well as by status code, so tightening the status-code oracle may not close the channel.
findings.summary: 409 account_unavailable is an account-existence oracle on an unauthenticated endpoint, in a service that goes to real lengths elsewhere to avoid being one (identical 401s, timing-equalised sign-in, no 403, no 410). The design node states this plainly and asks a reviewer to accept or reject it, so the security lens recorded it from the review side rather than re-arguing it: AC6 does require a visible refusal and there is no wording of one that is not a disclosure. What the lens pushes back on is the claim that the bucket makes it bounded - 60/min per IP is ~86,000 probes per address per day, and per SEC-2 it is unbounded whenever Redis is unreachable.

findings.suggestion: The design's rejection of DNS is defensible on TOCTOU grounds and the lens would not overturn it here. But record the residual gap where an operator will see it, and consider the cheap partial: refuse hosts whose canonical form ends in a label set known to be a loopback-mapping wildcard, or resolve at create time as a defence-in-depth signal that is allowed to fail open on lookup error. What would raise confidence that this is acceptable rather than an oversight is a line in artifacts/design.json or docs/OPERATIONS.md stating that name-to-internal-address targets are knowingly out of scope. Synthesis view: this is the one finding where the headline feature of the change is knowingly incomplete, and the anonymous endpoint widens who can exploit it - so the documentation line matters more now than it did when the decision was taken. It belongs in the same docs/OPERATIONS.md edit as SEC-5.
findings.summary: HostNormalizer closes textual and numeric equivalence well (the lens checked the trailing-dot, case, IDN, empty-label, hex/octal/short-form and out-of-range paths against java.net.URI's own host parsing and they hold, including the InetAddress.getByName('0177.0.0.1') trap the design calls out). But isInternal() returns false for anything that is not an IP literal and no DNS is resolved, so the simplest equivalent form of an internal address - a registered name that resolves to one - is still accepted: http://127.0.0.1.nip.io/, http://localtest.me/, or any attacker-controlled A record pointing at 127.0.0.1 or 169.254.169.254. The requirement's non-functional line asks the filter to resist equivalent-form evasion generally rather than only the two confirmed forms. Impact is bounded because nothing in this service fetches the target server-side (the lens grepped: no RestTemplate/WebClient/HttpClient/URLConnection anywhere in main), so this is not SSRF against us - the exposure is the clicker's own network, e.g. a corporate browser reaching an internal console via one of our links.

findings.suggestion: Confidence is low because the edge proxy very likely caps body size already (nginx client_max_body_size defaults to 1 MB) - confirming that cap and recording it in docs/OPERATIONS.md as a deployment precondition would close this finding without code. If the cap cannot be relied on, a small OncePerRequestFilter rejecting Content-Length above a few KB on these two paths is the in-service equivalent. Synthesis view: this is the third finding (with SEC-4 and SEC-5) whose resolution is a sentence in docs/OPERATIONS.md about what the edge proxy must do. That file was edited in this change and carries none of them. Treat the three as one documentation task, and note that if the edge proxy turns out not to preserve source addresses or cap bodies, several of this review's severity judgements move up together.
findings.summary: @Size(max = 2048) on longUrl (and @Size(max = 256) on SignUpRequest.password) is bean validation, which runs after Jackson has already materialised the whole string. Spring Boot applies no default size limit to a non-multipart, non-form request body, so an unauthenticated POST of a multi-hundred-megabyte JSON document to /api/v1/public/links or /api/v1/customers is fully parsed into heap before any constraint fires. Two new unauthenticated body-accepting endpoints widen a surface that previously existed only at POST /api/v1/sessions.

findings.suggestion: Make it a partial index: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_links_owner_listing_owned ON links (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) WHERE customer_id IS NOT NULL`, then drop the old one, in a follow-up migration (CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside Flyway's transaction - needs the mixed/non-transactional setting). Worth doing only once anonymous rows are a measurable fraction of the table; check with `SELECT count(*) FILTER (WHERE customer_id IS NULL), count(*) FROM links` and pg_relation_size on the index. Explicitly a follow-up, not a ship blocker - listed near the end of the minors for that reason. It is the same measurement PERF-7 asks for, so instrument once and let the number decide both.
findings.summary: ix_links_owner_listing (customer_id, created_at DESC, code ASC) will now index anonymous rows it can never serve: every owner-scoped query is an equality match on customer_id and SQL equality never matches NULL, so each anonymous link adds an index entry that no query can read. On the busiest table in the system, at a permitted 30 creates/min/IP with no reaper, that is monotonic index growth for zero read benefit - larger index, slower vacuum, more buffer cache spent on unreachable tuples. Impact is proportional to anonymous adoption, which nobody can estimate yet; at low volume it is invisible.

findings.suggestion: Ship a metric before the endpoint gets traffic: gauge `links` row count split by customer_id IS NULL, and total relation size, on the existing Prometheus endpoint. Decide a retention policy for expired anonymous rows (archive-then-delete keeping the code reserved) if the anonymous share passes some agreed fraction of the table. Synthesis view: the instrumentation half is worth doing now even though the policy half is not - it is cheap, it is the same measurement PERF-5 needs, and it is the only way anyone will find out whether either finding matters. Shipping an unauthenticated write endpoint with no gauge on what it writes is the part that should not wait.
findings.summary: Anonymous links expire after 30 days but are never removed: V1 states 'nothing is ever deleted' and there is no reaper, so an anonymous row occupies the links table, the ux_links_domain_code index and the (domain, code) namespace permanently while being unredirectable after a month and undeletable by anyone (no owner, no admin endpoint). The migration comment names 'let the TTL drain' as the rollback plan, which is true of redirect behaviour but not of storage. The performance lens could not size this from the code - it depends entirely on adoption of an endpoint that has never been exposed - so it is flagged as something to watch rather than something to fix now. The security lens reached the same observation from the other side and consciously classified it as capacity rather than security, so two lenses saw it and neither could bound it.

findings.suggestion: Add `private String shortUrl(String code)` and use it from both toResponse and the AnonymousLinkResponse construction; keep the two response builders separate since the DTOs genuinely differ. Same one-line-extraction shape as CLEAN-1 and in the same method, so do them together; this one is a nit because the duplicated expression carries no security or acceptance-criterion weight, whereas CLEAN-1's does.
findings.summary: createAnonymous builds its response inline while every other read path in the class goes through toResponse, and `baseUrl + "/" + link.getCode()` is now spelled in two places. The short-URL join is the sort of thing that acquires trailing-slash handling later in one copy only.

findings.suggestion: Truncate to ChronoUnit.MICROS in LinkService as SignUpService already does, so the created-response value is the value that is stored and read back. Listed first among the nits because it is the smallest fix in the review, the correct pattern already exists two files away with a comment explaining it, and a client that caches the create response and compares it to a later read is a plausible thing to exist.
findings.summary: Timestamp precision is inconsistent across responses for the same resource. SignUpService truncates to microseconds (SignUpService.java:57 - I confirmed the truncatedTo(ChronoUnit.MICROS) call and its comment) so the body matches what the TIMESTAMP(6) column will return, but LinkService.create/createAnonymous use a raw Instant.now(), so the 201 body carries nanosecond precision (e.g. ...T12:00:00.123456789Z) while a later GET /api/v1/links/{code} returns the rounded stored value (...123457Z). Both are valid ISO-8601 instants per openapi.yaml line 152, so this is not a schema break, but createdAt/expiresAt for one link differ between the create response and every subsequent read.

findings.suggestion: If it is worth keeping, pin it where it is observable: a unit test calling DenylistThreatCheck.evaluate directly with URI.create("http://4294967296/") and asserting ThreatVerdict.BLOCK, independent of the validator having run first. Synthesis view: keep it and pin it. The security lens independently confirmed that both call sites fail closed on Optional.empty() and treated that as one of the reasons the normalisation work is sound - so this branch is load-bearing for a conclusion elsewhere in the review even though no endpoint reaches it, and pruning it later would quietly invalidate that reasoning. Same theme as CLEAN-1: correctness that currently rests on call order or on duplicated prose rather than on structure.
findings.summary: The fail-closed branch added here (canonical.isEmpty() -> BLOCK) is unreachable through any endpoint: UrlValidator.requireShortenable already throws url_rejected on an un-canonicalisable host before the threat check runs, so no test would notice if this branch were deleted. Its own comment states the point - 'a security property that holds only because they run in a particular order is one reordering away from not holding' - and that property, independence from ordering, is precisely what no test asserts. Defence in depth deliberately added, recorded so it is a decision rather than dead code somebody later prunes.

findings.suggestion: Annotate the method @ResourceLock(Resources.LOCALE) so JUnit serialises it if parallel execution is ever enabled, and leave the assertion as it is. One annotation, no behaviour change - the cheapest item in the review, and the Turkish-locale case is exactly the kind of test worth protecting from being deleted the first time someone chases a flake.
findings.summary: caseIsNotPartOfAHost mutates JVM-global state (Locale.setDefault('tr')) to prove the lower-casing is locale-independent. It is restored in a finally and there is no junit-platform.properties enabling parallelism, so it is safe today - but it is a shared-JVM global in a suite that boots Spring contexts, and the day parallel execution is turned on this becomes order-dependent flakiness in whatever else happens to format a string. The behaviour is worth pinning; the hazard is worth declaring.

findings.suggestion: Have valueOf take the radix as a parameter (the caller can obtain it once) and return OptionalLong, or keep the long sentinel but name it (`private static final long NOT_AN_ADDRESS_PART = -1L`) so the two failure encodings are at least both self-describing. Handle with care: this is the hand-rolled numeric parser at the centre of the change, the security lens checked its behaviour against java.net.URI case by case and found it correct, and the test lens explicitly did not audit the 147-line body against the unit expectations. A readability refactor of code that two lenses have verified only from the outside is worth doing only with the unit suite green before and after, and probably not in the same change as the functional fixes above.
findings.summary: Two different sentinel conventions live within twenty lines: radixOf returns NOT_A_NUMBER (0) and valueOf returns -1, so asDottedQuad has to test `part < 0` for one failure and callers test `== NOT_A_NUMBER` for the other. valueOf also recomputes radixOf for a part isAddressCandidate has already classified, so the classification exists twice.

findings.suggestion: Either rename to SignUpController to match SignInController and its service, or leave it and accept that customer-resource endpoints belong here. Worth one line either way; the current pairing is the only inconsistency. Last in the reading order deliberately: it is the only finding in the review with no defect behind it at all, filed by its own lens at low confidence as a note for whoever adds the second customer endpoint.
findings.summary: CustomerController is named for the resource while its immediate sibling SignInController is named for the action, and it delegates to SignUpService. Nothing is wrong today - one endpoint, one collaborator - but the name promises the customer resource generally, so the next customer endpoint (GET /customers/{id}, password change) will land here by name rather than by cohesion.

summary: Five lenses filed 33 findings and no blockers; I have merged one pair, promoted two findings to blocker, and lowered nothing. The change itself is strong — HostNormalizer is the headline and the security lens could not break it, the redirect hot path is byte-identical, no existing test was touched (132 methods before, 242 after), and every documented status and body the contract lens could check by reading is honoured. The single thing to look at first is SEC-1: AC4 turns every authenticated endpoint from two hand-provisioned accounts into anyone with an HTTP client, and the one capability that deliberately crosses tenant lines is the immediate, unmoderated, irreversible abuse-report takedown, whose only limit is keyed on a customer id an attacker now mints at 60/min — impact.json rated that flow "low" on a premise this change makes vacuous. Two things should pause the pipeline: SEC-1, because the capability is irreversible by design and needs a product decision rather than a reviewer's; and TEST-1, because AC3 requires tests observed failing against the pre-change code, author-tests and implement ran in parallel and the suite first executed after the join, so that evidence does not exist and a downstream node would otherwise mark AC3 met on a green post-fix run. Both promotions are mine, not the lenses'. Below the blockers, four majors cluster on the two new unauthenticated write paths — a lower(email) index that cannot serve the upper() predicate sign-in actually issues, an Argon2 hash with no concurrency ceiling, a pooled connection held across a Redis call, and a fail-open limiter that removes the only bound on all three at once — and the twenty minors are mostly one-sitting fixes and three deployment preconditions that belong in a single docs/OPERATIONS.md edit.
top_risks: No lens executed anything. All five not_examined lists say so explicitly — no build, no load test, no profiler, no query plan, no suite run, no live request. Every status code, index-usage claim, lock class, framework default and flakiness judgement in this document is read from source. The only execution in the whole pipeline was maven_verify at the verify node, and TEST-1 establishes that it ran only against the fixed code. The release gate should treat this review as static analysis by five readers, not as verification.

Every quantitative bound in this review is conditional on two facts nobody established. First, Redis being reachable: the limiter fails open by design, so '60/min per IP' and '30/min per IP' become 'unbounded' during exactly the outage where the service is least able to absorb it (SEC-2). Second, the edge proxy preserving the source address: if it does not, both new buckets are single global ceilings and provide no per-attacker protection at all (SEC-5). Fixing every finding below leaves both conditions unverified, and several severities move up together if either turns out false.

redis/token_bucket.lua was read by nobody — the API, security and test lenses each list it as not examined, and the performance lens assumed Lettuce's failure behaviour from a timeout value in config. The rate limiter is the sole mitigation cited in SEC-1, SEC-2, SEC-7, PERF-2 and PERF-4, and its refill arithmetic and atomicity are unreviewed. This is the largest single hole in the review itself.

Whether the two new per-IP buckets are genuinely per-caller is untested from both directions: every test in the suite originates from loopback (test lens), and the deployment precondition that would make the key meaningful is absent from the runbook that was edited in this change (SEC-5). AC14 is therefore unevidenced rather than met.

The V3/V4 migrations have never been rehearsed against a production-shaped database. Lock classes were reasoned from statement type, not observed; the duplicate-address precondition that aborts V3 is unfalsifiable from this repository and only recorded in docs/TODO.md; and on the shipped ordering that abort leaves a half-migrated database in which the new anonymous path cannot write (API-4, PERF-6). Three lenses touched these files and none could test them.

The trust-boundary change is a product decision that no individual fix undoes. Self-service sign-up re-scopes every authenticated endpoint at once; SEC-1, SEC-7, SEC-8 and SEC-6 are four consequences that happened to be noticed. Nothing in this pipeline re-derived the threat model after AC4, and impact.json's risk register still reflects the two-account world — that stale artefact is not itself any lens's finding.

Storage growth from unauthenticated writes is unbounded and unowned. Anonymous links expire in 30 days but are never deleted, have no owner and no admin endpoint; customers grows without limit from an open endpoint. The performance lens filed it, the security lens saw it and classified it as capacity, and neither could size it because the endpoint has never carried traffic. No gauge ships with the feature, so the first measurement will be an incident.

Several surfaces sit outside every lens's brief: the actuator endpoints (health, info, metrics, prometheus) are exposed outside the session filter and the contract declares no operations for them, so nobody compared them against anything; no SCA or CVE scan was run against jjwt, Spring Boot 3.5, the Argon2 provider or the Redis client; TLS, CORS and security response headers have no representation in this repository; docker-compose.yml was not read for default credentials or exposed ports; and the JWT's own claims, issuer and 24-hour expiry were not traced into JwtIssuer/JwtVerifier.
